The House of Medici. They rose from merchant banking to become the de facto rulers of Florence and one of Renaissance Europe's most influential families. Though they rarely held an official title, the Medici wielded immense political power through wealth and patronage, cultivating some of the greatest artists, scholars, and thinkers of the Italian Renaissance.

Cosimo de Medici, living from 1389 to 1464, began the family's dominance as wealthy merchant bankers in Florence. Though technically a private citizen, he became the city's most powerful man. His great-grandson, Lorenzo the Magnificent, born in 1449 and dying in 1492, perfected the art of power-brokering without formal title. He was a diplomat, patron, and poet who made Florence a cultural epicenter.

The Medici wielded power through accumulated wealth from banking, cloth trade, and political alliances with popes and foreign rulers. They married into European nobility and the papacy itself. As supreme patrons of the Italian Renaissance, they commissioned Michelangelo's David and Sistine Chapel, Botticelli's works, and Leonardo da Vinci's innovations. Cosimo I reigned from 1537 to 1574 and became the first Grand Duke of Tuscany, elevating the family to formal princely rank. His successors ruled Tuscany until 1737. The Medici also produced two queens of France—Catherine de Medici, who married Henry II, and Marie de Medici, who married Henry IV.
